Local Tastes
Sarmale
Romania's signature comfort dish — minced pork and rice wrapped in pickled cabbage or vine leaves, slow-simmered in tomato broth, and served with sour cream and polenta.
Traditional restaurants · find nearby
Mici
Grilled ground-meat rolls made from a blend of beef, pork, and lamb with garlic and spices — always served with mustard and flatbread; ubiquitous at street markets and traditional restaurants.
Street markets & cârciumi city-wide · find nearby
Ciorbă de burtă
Tripe soup soured with vinegar or sauerkraut brine, enriched with sour cream and garlic — Bucharest's classic late-night restorative, served at traditional cârciumi.
Traditional cârciumi city-wide · find nearby
Cozonac
A sweet, enriched braided bread filled with walnuts, cocoa, or poppy seeds — traditionally baked for Orthodox Easter and Christmas; sold year-round at Bucharest bakeries.
Bucharest bakeries city-wide · find nearby
Țuică
Romania's national spirit — a double-distilled plum brandy, drunk straight and neat before meals; every traditional restaurant in Bucharest carries a house bottle.
Traditional restaurants city-wide · find nearby

Day Trips by Train
Sinaia · 1 hr 20 min
A Carpathian mountain resort town built around Peleș Castle — a neo-Renaissance royal palace set in pine forests at 800 m elevation; also home to Pelișor Castle and the Sinaia Monastery. Regional trains run hourly.
book at: Trainline or Omio
Brașov · 2 hr 30 min
A medieval Saxon city in the Carpathian foothills — the Gothic Black Church, a walled old town, and Bran Castle a short taxi ride away. Fast InterCity trains available.
book at: Trainline or Omio

Worth Knowing

A former Paris of the East, still rebuilding its story

Bucharest was called "the Paris of the East" — not as flattery but as plain description. The boulevards, the Belle Époque façades on Calea Victoriei, the Athenaeum modelled on the Paris Opéra, the covered arcades: all of it was built with a specific city in mind. Nicolae Ceaușescu spent a decade demolishing a third of it. What you walk through today is the city held together by what survived, with cranes still on some of the gaps.

That tension makes Bucharest unlike anywhere else in Europe. The Palace of the Parliament is genuinely staggering — not beautiful, but impossible to ignore, and the sheer scale of it tells you something about what the communist decades cost. The Old Town blocks away are the opposite: small, human, with the Stavropoleos carving and the old beer hall at Caru' cu Bere reminding you what the city was before the bulldozers came. One day covers both, which is rare. Most European cities keep their history in one register; Bucharest forces you to hold two very different ones at once.
